sessions.title: Whistleblower Protection Strategies
sessions.description: The stakes for whistleblowers have grown exponentially in recent years, with the might of government and private companies time and again mobilized to identify and punish those who speak out of school to expose wrongdoing. In the most serious cases, prosecutors are increasingly invoking the Espionage Act, which carries a potential life sentence. This workshop with unpack methods for minimizing risk for whistleblowers, and for the journalists and filmmakers who rely on their disclosures. It is important to understand the risks for the journalists and filmmakers to pro-actively and as safely as possible work with whistleblowers.

sessions.title: Fact Checking
sessions.description:
In an era in which fake news and filter bubbles seem to create alternative realities and threaten the basis of democracy, it’s more important than ever that investigative journalism is factually correct, so viewers can trust the reporting.

In this workshop presented by the Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting, we will show what can happen if journalists and news organizations neglect to fact-check before publishing or for the sake of dramatic storytelling omit important facts. This is a hands-on workshop; we will train participants to strategically and efficiently fact-check their own biases and their own reporting, even if the filmmaker has no institutional support. We will show how to independently verify facts, background people and use new tools that can help verify when and where an image was shot. Filmmakers will not only develop a road map to fact-check their own work, they will also learn about investigative skills and tools that will benefit any reporting, and even facilitate distribution.

sessions.title: Solutions Journalism for Investigative Film
sessions.description: Participants in this interactive workshop will learn how to use solutions journalism to add audience appeal and real-world impact to an investigative film. They’ll learn: The What: What is solutions journalism — and what is it not? The Why: How can solutions journalism make a documentary film stronger? The How: How do I find a solutions angle? How do I report on a solution without advocacy, cheerleading, do-gooding or PR? How do I integrate it into a problem-focused story?

sessions.title: The Art of Exposure with Halcyon House Fellows
sessions.description: Each year, Double Exposure celebrates the vibrant intersection of investigative journalism and film. The cinematic lens, though, is but one medium in which investigative journalism influences and shapes the cultural landscape. This year’s symposium incorporates podcasts that have broken new investigative ground on their own. With this session, we’re proud to partner with Halcyon House Arts Lab. This session will present Halcyon fellows-in-residence whose work is fueled by deep reporting on timely issues. Through performance, photography, poetry, and other forms of art they tackle the quest to expose and investigate from new directions. The artists will present segments from their work in a series of presentations, and be on hand to take questions.

sessions.title: Grant Writing Workshop
sessions.description: In the Grant Writing Master Class, IDA’s Program Officer Dana Merwin outlines the multi-faceted grant-writing process for documentary projects. From the Fiscal Sponsorship program, which has supported documentary production and post-production for nearly 30 years, to the specialized funding of the Pare Lorentz Documentary Fund and the Enterprise Documentary Fund, she uses IDA’s funding opportunities as a starting point to discuss the fundamentals of writing a strong application. She also chats with IDA Pare Lorentz grantee Heidi Reinberg, whose film, 93Queen, offers an in-depth case study of how to weave your film’s loglines, synopsis, treatments and more into a compelling package for potential funders. As a special feature of this class, Dana workshops the loglines of projects brought forth by attendees.

sessions.title: Finding Character
sessions.description: From the unstoppable growth of podcasting to the latest binge-worthy formats in storytelling to new ways of engaging your audience, all of them require a creative approach to your investigation. Join Susanne Reber for a wide-ranging conversation to explore how you can prepare yourself to think in characters, scenes, and sequences and allow your story to make it into video or audio and sometimes both. We will talk about the mindset, casting your characters early on, and finding creative ways to solve familiar challenges in investigative reporting: complexity, data sets, and numbers. How can you frame your story to engage your audience, hold its attention and build their involvement, by using available technology to start a two-way conversation?

sessions.title: Defy Apathy! A Workshop to Build Public Trust in Journalism
sessions.description:
A hands-on session in which attendees of the symposium use creative tools to find solutions to truth decay and restoring public trust in the news.

The workshop is facilitated by Eric Matthies, filmmaker, and narrative design producer. Eric has a longstanding involvement in citizen advocacy for the press and experience convening disparate stakeholders in active sessions to build stable solutions for complex problems.

The session kicks off with a brief introduction/presentation of researched facts defining the problem and its core drivers. Then, each of our invited media representatives will engage in moderated discussion on the topic from their perspective, after which we’ll divide into groups and use narrative design tools and some punk ‘Do It Yourself’ energy to prototype art-based solutions.

The most important expert in the room is you – this is an opportunity where we working professionals and the public come together around our respective areas of expertise and concern to help build solutions. Rebuilding trust in journalism is not for journalism, it is for all of us – we are explicitly and intrinsically entangled with a need for trustworthy information.

For the majority of time in the session, we will split into working groups moderated by each of our experts and guided by the workshop facilitator. Taking advantage of the spectrum of creative tools available to us at Double Exposure will ensure a stimulating experience with a tangible outcome. What we make and how we define, design and execute it will be largely up to the convened group of participants. At the end of the session, everyone will have contributed to making contextual, illuminating and actionable content that each participant can share via their own platforms.

people.name: Sobia Ahmad
people.bio: Sobia Ahmad was born and raised in Pakistan, and moved to the United States at the age of fourteen. Highlighting the inseparability of the self and larger power structures, her interdisciplinary work dissects how spiritual, social, and historical, shape intimate personal narratives and broader community experiences. A strong believer in the power of art for social justice, Ahmad explores how our deeply intimate struggles of belonging can inform larger conversations about national identity, notion of home, cultural memory, and gender.

people.name: Alex Braden
people.bio: Alex Braden was born in Detroit and studied classical piano from age four and jazz guitar from age eleven. He taught freelance through college where he eventually abandoned a music scholarship to pursue a BFA in Sound Art. Later, between recording and touring with three bands, Braden further developed his fine art practice: experimenting with interactive and immersive. He shares a space in Northeast Washington, DC with his painter–wife Amy and budding noise–artist–toddler, Quincy.

people.name: Halim Flowers
people.bio: Halim Flowers was arrested at the age of 16 and sentenced as an adult to two life sentences in DC. In the year of 2005, he started his own publishing company SATO Communications, through which he published 11 books. In 2018, he co-founded the social entrepreneurial media production company Unchained Media Collective with filmmaker Kristin Adair to disrupt mass incarceration with the stories of those that are directly impacted by the criminal justice system. On March 21, 2019, Halim was released from prison after serving 22 years imprisoned. He uses his writings, motivational speeches, and fitness routines to inspire people towards revolutionary love.

people.name: Ashley M Freeby
people.bio: Ashley M Freeby is a multidisciplinary artist who was born in rural Pennsylvania and currently lives in Chicago, IL. Freeby uses her voice to project truth telling works through a multitude of mediums. Focusing on the history of land, she questions who worked it, who owned it and the accessibility of it. Freeby uses natural materials, poetic language and minimalist aesthetics to explore sites of trauma and challenge our perceptions of memory of lives lost. She earned a MFA from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago (2018) and a BA from Bucknell University (2015).

people.name: Molly Joyce
people.bio: Molly Joyce is a celebrated composer and performer whose work is primarily concerned with disability as a creative source. Through compositions, performances, video, and research, she generates material which reimagines disability and loss of physicality. Molly often sings and plays with her vintage toy organ, an instrument she loves due to how it fits her physically-impaired left hand. Molly has studied at The Juilliard School, Royal Conservatory in The Hague, and Yale School of Music.

people.name: Lionel Frazier White III
people.bio: Lionel Frazier White III is a D.C native who is a passionate arts educator and interdisciplinary conceptual artist. He is a graduate of The George Washington University Corcoran school of art and design with his BFA in fine art. White is a Washington DC-based artist who works in painting, drawing, wood sculpture, installation, and mixed media collage. White’s work explores themes of forced and coerced labor affects family pathology, erasure, displacement, reassertion, and gentrification.

people.name: Janae Williams
people.bio: Janae Williams is a dreamer, doer and diviner deeply committed to the transformative and contagious power of being whole. In the ancient legacy of the multitude of black femmehood, Janae she is a: photographer, digital visual artist and DJ. She is the creative co-director and lead organizer of the DC-based, Black Femme Brunch, a community which cultivates radical, irreverent and unapologetic celebration of black trans and queer femmes of all (or no) genders.

people.name: Stephanie J Woods
people.bio: Stephanie J Woods is a Charlotte, NC based artist creating textile, photography, and community engaged projects. Through the use of symbolic mediums referencing black American culture and the southern experience, her multimedia works examine the cognitive effects of cultural assimilation, and how performance is ingrained in identity. Woods earned an MFA in Studio Art from the University of North Carolina at Greensboro and has served as faculty at Virginia Commonwealth University, and in 2017 her work was notably recognized by the South Arts Fellowship, and NC. Arts Council Fellowship.

people.name: Laila Al-Arian
people.bio: Laila Al-Arian is a Washington-based journalist and senior producer for Fault Lines, an award-winning current affairs program on Al Jazeera English. She has produced documentaries on subjects ranging from the Trump administration's Muslim ban to abortion restrictions in the U.S., the heroin epidemic's impact on children, and factory conditions in Bangladesh. Laila worked for Al Jazeera English for four years, covering everything from Guantanamo Bay’s youngest detainee to the resettlement of Iraqi refugees in the U.S. Her work has appeared in The Nation, Salon, The Independent, and other publications.

people.name: Anne Alvergue
people.bio: Anne Alvergue is an award-winning documentary filmmaker and editor. Her short films have screened internationally at film festivals and galleries, including the Pacific Film Archive, Galapagos Gallery, San Francisco Art Institute, Arsenal Berlin, Black Maria, Mill Valley, and Centro De La Imagen. Her editing credits include Love, Gilda; Bully. Coward. Victim: The Story of Roy Cohn; That Way Madness Lies, Museum Town, Being Elmo, Life After Hoop Dreams, Tibet in Song, My Kid Could Paint That, and Married in America. Anne received a Bachelor’s Degree from UC Berkeley and a Master’s Degree in Documentary Film from Stanford University.

people.name: Karim Amer
people.bio: Karim Amer is an Egyptian-American filmmaker based in New York City best known for producing the documentary, The Square (AL MIDAN) (2013). The film was nominated for an Academy Award and received Emmy Awards for Directing, Cinematography, and Editing in 2014. Karim also produced the award-winning documentary, Rafea: Solar Mama (2013), and teamed up with Angelina Jolie to executive produce the Academy Award nominated animated feature, The Breadwinner (2017). His most recent film, The Great Hack, premiered at the 2019 Sundance Film Festival and launched globally on Netflix on July 24th of this year. He is currently in production on a documentary series for HBO about NXIVM.

people.name: Nathalie Applewhite
people.bio: Nathalie Applewhite is the managing director of the Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting, a nonprofit journalism organization dedicated to promoting in-depth engagement with global affairs. She has played a key role in the development of the Center's model and approach towards journalism initiatives, multimedia development and educational outreach. She was the managing producer on a number of the Center’s interactive projects, including the Emmy award-winning LiveHopeLove.

people.name: Patricia Aufderheide
people.bio: Patricia Aufderheide is University Professor of Communication Studies in the School of Communication at American University in Washington, D.C. She founded the School's Center for Media & Social Impact, where she continues as Senior Research Fellow. Her books include Reclaiming Fair Use: How to Put Balance Back in Copyright (University of Chicago), with Peter Jaszi; Documentary: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford), The Daily Planet (University of Minnesota Press), and Communications Policy in the Public Interest (Guilford Press). She has been a Fulbright Research Fellow twice, in Brazil (1994-5) and Australia (2017).

people.name: Edward Baker
people.bio: Edward Baker is Counsel in Constantine Cannon’s DC office. He represents whistleblowers under the False Claims Act. He previously served as an AUSA in CA, and cares deeply about the role of whistleblowers in fostering transparency in government.

people.name: Neela Banerjee
people.bio: Neela Banerjee is a Washington-based reporter for Inside Climate News. She led the investigation into Exxon's early climate research, which was a finalist for the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service reporting and the recipient of nearly a dozen other journalism awards. Before joining ICN, she spent four years as the energy and environmental reporter for the Los Angeles Times' Washington bureau. Banerjee covered global energy, the Iraq War and other issues with The New York Times. She also served as a Moscow correspondent with The Wall Street Journal. Banerjee grew up in southeast Louisiana and graduated from Yale University.

people.name: Alexia Bedat
people.bio: Alexia Bedat focuses her practice on content review, media law, privacy, internet law, advertising, fair use, and virtual and augmented reality technologies. Prior to joining Klaris Law, Ms. Bedat worked as a law clerk at BuzzFeed, where she supported the news team. She has also worked with law firms specializing in media law in both London and Paris. She is an AR&VR enthusiast and frequently addresses legal challenges in this area, most recently at SXSW in Austin, TX (2018), the Augmented World Expo in Santa Clara, CA (2018) and AR in Action at MIT (2019).

people.name: Laura Beil
people.bio: Laura Beil is an independent journalist specializing in medicine, health policy and science. She was the recipient of the Victor Cohn Prize for Medical Science Reporting in 2018. In addition to being a contributing correspondent at Science News, her work has appeared in numerous publications, including The New York Times, Cosmopolitan, Reader's Digest, Men's Health, and other magazines. She began freelancing in 2007 after working as a medical writer for the Dallas Morning News from 1992 to 2006. In 2018, she reported and hosted the podcast Dr. Death, which has been downloaded more than 50 million times.

people.name: Robin Bell
people.bio: Robin Bell, founder of Bell Visuals, is an award-winning editor, video journalist, and multimedia artist based in Washington, DC. In 2005, he co-produced Operation Ceasefire, a seminal anti-war concert on the National Mall. His feature-length documentary, Positive Force: More Than a Witness: 30 Years of Punk Politics In Action, premiered in 2014. Bell is the director and producer of the Directed Actions Live Film Series and creates permanent public art installations in addition to his ongoing work with ephemeral media forms.

people.name: Suzette Brewer
people.bio: Suzette Brewer is a writer specializing in federal Indian law, having written extensively on the Indian Child Welfare Act, environmental issues on reservations, the opioid crisis in Indian Country and violence against Native women and children for The Dallas Morning News, The Denver Post, and many others. Her published books include Real Indians: Portraits of Contemporary Native Americans and America's Tribal Colleges; Sovereign: An Oral History of Indian Gaming in America. She is the 2015 recipient of the Richard LaCourse-Gannett Foundation Al Neuharth Investigative Journalism Award for her work on the Indian Child Welfare Act. She is also a 2018 John Jay/Tow Juvenile Justice Reporting Fellow.

people.name: Natalie Bullock Brown
people.bio: Natalie Bullock Brown is the lead strategist of StoryShift, a program of Working Films committed to shifting the way stories are told to ensure accountable and authentic representation of the people and the places featured. She is currently working on her first feature-length documentary film as a director, which will explore beauty standards and their impact on black women and girls. Natalie served as host of Black Issues Forum, a public affairs program on UNC-TV. Natalie maintained a freelance career, providing production, research, and rights clearance consultation for award-winning filmmakers and prestigious media companies and more. Before going freelance, Natalie served as a producer and reporter for UNC-TV.

people.name: Katie Campbell
people.bio: Katie Campbell is an Emmy and Edward R. Murrow award-winning filmmaker and journalist at ProPublica. She produces in-depth science stories and recently won a 2019 National Academies of Sciences Keck Communications Award for a project on how levees make flooding worse. Prior to joining ProPublica, she managed video for a CPB-funded public-media environmental reporting partnership, where her investigation into the illegal exportation of electronic waste helped uncover the largest e-recycling fraud in U.S. history. She holds a master’s degree in narrative journalism from the University of Oregon.

people.name: Kenyatta Cheese
people.bio: Kenyatta Cheese is a professional internet enthusiast. As co-founder of the audience development agency Everybody at Once, he gets creators to reframe the producer-consumer relationship as systems of participation. As co-creator of the internet meme database Know Your Meme, he has helped the web better understand itself as a vital space of emergent culture. In previous iterations he has worked with the Eyebeam Center for Art and Technology, Manhattan Neighborhood Network, and the online video network Rocketboom.

people.name: Erika Cheung
people.bio: Erika Cheung was one of the key whistleblowers in the Theranos scandal that stopped the company from processing thousands of patients samples with faulty technology, which has been covered in the book Bad Blood by John Carreyrou, 60 minutes, ABC news, and recently the HBO documentary The Inventor: Out for Blood in the Silicon Valley. Prior to that, she committed herself to grow the entrepreneurial ecosystem in Hong Kong, China, and South East Asia, and spearheaded the foundation of the Betatron, a technology accelerator based in Hong Kong. She founded Spiral Bio, an application-based community facilitating investment and partnerships for healthcare and biotechnology companies across the APAC markets.

people.name: Carrie Cochran
people.bio: Carrie Cochran is a filmmaker and journalist for the Scripps Washington Bureau's investigative team. She worked on the film A Broken Trust, that examines the high prevalence of sexual assault on tribal lands and the federal government’s involvement in the criminal justice on two reservations in the Great Plains. In 2018, Cochran was also the lead producer, lead editor and a cinematographer for the 30-minute documentary Seven Days of Heroin, that was awarded the Pulitzer Prize and National Murrow Award. The National Press Photographers Association named Cochran among the top photojournalism multimedia producers internationally for her video work.

people.name: Michael Connor
people.bio: Michael Connor is Program Associate for the Park Foundation, working chiefly with the Media program. He came to Park in 2015 after a long career in journalism. After graduating from Cornell University in 1975, he began newspaper work as a reporter for The Post-Standard in Syracuse, NY, and eventually became managing editor and executive editor of the paper. In 1988-89, he spent a year at Harvard as a Nieman Fellow before returning to the newsroom in Syracuse. During his tenure, The Post-Standard was one of three finalists for a Pulitzer Prize in explanatory reporting for a months-long investigation of shoddy health care in New York State’s prison system, a series that led to reforms in Albany. He left the newspaper in 2013 to spend a year in southern France and upon returning to the US, assisted with the launch of a nonprofit digital news operation in Ithaca.

people.name: Brenda Coughlin
people.bio: Brenda Coughlin is the Director of Producing and Impact Strategy for Sundance Institute. She is part of the Sundance Creative Producing Program and a staff advisor to various granting funds. Brenda’s projects as an independent producer include Academy Award-nominated Dirty Wars (2013), and Laura Poitras’ last two features: CITIZENFOUR (2014), and Risk (2016). She produced Poitras’ 2016 solo exhibition, and Astro Noise, at the Whitney Museum of American Art. With the late historian Howard Zinn, she co-founded the performing arts non-profit Voices of a People’s History, and also produced The People Speak live event documentary series, along with executive producer Matt Damon.

people.name: Lindsay Crouse
people.bio: Lindsay Crouse is the coordinating producer for The New York Times Op-Docs series. Since joining Op-Docs in 2011, she has worked on nearly 300 short films, VR, and interactive documentaries that won two Emmy Awards, two Peabodys, and two Oscar nominations for best short documentary.

people.name: Angelica Das
people.bio: Angelica Das is the Senior Program Associate for Engaged Journalism in the Public Square Program at the Democracy Fund, a bipartisan foundation working to ensure that our political system is able to withstand new challenges and deliver on its promise to the American people. She was previously a senior associate with Dot Connector Studio, who collaborates with funders, journalists, and experts to research, develop and produce social impact media projects. Angelica specialized in developing and fostering communities of practice for documentary film, public media, investigative journalism, engaged journalism, and others.

people.name: Ramona S. Diaz
people.bio: Ramona S. Diaz is an award-winning Asian American filmmaker whose films have ranged in other top-tier film festivals such as Sundance, the Berlinale, Tribeca, and the list goes on. All of Ramona's feature-length films include Imelda (2004), The Learning (2011), Don’t Stop Believin’: Everyman’s Journey (2012) and her latest film, Motherland (2017), which have all been broadcast on PBS. Motherland won an award at the 2017 Sundance Film Festival and it was nominated for an Independent Spirit Award for best Documentary, a Peabody Award, and a Gawad Urian Award from the Filipino Film Critics.

people.name: Wendy Ettinger
people.bio: Wendy Ettinger has been producing narrative films and documentaries for over 20 years. In 2005, she co-founded Chicken & Egg Pictures to fund and mentor women documentary directors whose artful and innovative storytelling catalyzes social change, awarding $7 million in grants and thousands of hours of creative mentorship to approximately 300 filmmakers. In 2013, Wendy co-founded Gamechanger Films, the first equity fund established to finance and invest in woman narrative directors. Gamechanger Films 2 will launch in early 2020.

people.name: Margaux Ewen
people.bio: Margaux Ewen is the executive director of the James W. Foley Legacy Foundation, a non-profit organization founded after the brutal 2014 murder of James Foley, an American freelance journalist, while he was held captive by ISIS in Syria. The foundation’s mission is to advocate for the freedom of all Americans held hostage or unjustly detained abroad and promote the safety of journalists worldwide. The Foundation works with the families of Americans held abroad to push the US government to prioritize their return, and works with educational institutions to develop and implement journalism safety curricula for students of journalism across the country.

people.name: Feras Fayyad
people.bio: Feras Fayyad is an award-winning filmmaker who has received particular recognition for his work on contemporary Syrian issues and the political transformation of the Arab world. His most recent film, “Last Men in Aleppo,” earned him a 2018 Academy Award nomination for Best Documentary Feature. The film followed a small group of volunteer rescue workers with the White Helmets civil defense organization. “Last Men in Aleppo” premiered at the 2017 Sundance Film Festival, where it won the Grand Jury Prize in the World Cinema Documentary competition. The film went on to screen at festivals around the globe and received numerous international awards.

people.name: Lauren Feeney
people.bio: Lauren Feeney leads the video team at The Intercept, an online outlet focusing on investigative and adversarial journalism. In addition to The Intercept, her work has been featured on air and online at The New York Times, PBS and Al Jazeera English among other outlets, and in film festivals and events around the world. She divides her time between New York and Boston.

people.name: Jennifer Forde
people.bio: Jennifer Forde worked for many years as a television documentary producer, both inside the BBC and at several leading UK production companies. Her impressive litany of credits includes directing and producing on a Royal Television Society Award winning BBC Four documentary series about the national grid, a Grierson-short-listed documentary series about Catholic identity in Britain, and working with Louis Theroux on his series LA Stories. West Cork was her first journey into an audio-exclusive format. Working with Sam Bungey, they then followed up with a podcast series about the UK punk band The Clash, narrated by Chuck D, and serialised earlier this year on Spotify.

people.name: Casey Frank
people.bio: Casey Frank is the senior editor for investigations and enterprise at the Miami Herald. He previously co-founded the weekly Lincoln Park News on the North Side of Chicago. In addition to editing Perversion of Justice, on the travails of Jeffrey Epstein, he was the Herald's editor or co-editor on the Panama Papers, which shared a Pulitzer winner with the International Center for Investigative Journalists and McClatchy, as well as Fight Club (on Florida juvenile justice) and Dirty Gold, Clean Cash (on the plunder of the South American rain forest by gold miners) both Pulitzer finalists over the past two years.

people.name: Theodore Frank
people.bio: Theodore Frank is a Retired Partner at Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer. He graduated at the University of Texas School of Law in 1966, where he was an editor of the Law Review. He subsequently clerked for Judge Walter P. Gewin of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit and then was Faculty Assistant for the Ames Competition at Law School, where he earned an LL.M. Frank has been practicing communications law for over 45 years.

people.name: Samara Freemark
people.bio: Samara Freemark is the Co-Creator and Senior Producer of APM Reports’ investigative podcast In the Dark. Prior to that role, she covered education and veterans' issues for American Public Media, worked as a reporter and producer with Radio Diaries, and worked in the newsroom of WUOM Ann Arbor. She’s a two-time recipient of the George Foster Peabody Award, as well as the George Polk Award and other awards. She holds a B.A. from Swarthmore College and an M.A. in Urban Planning from the University of Michigan.

people.name: Cassandra Giraldo
people.bio: Cassandra Giraldo is a photojournalist and produced shot long-form, immersive feature stories including “World of Hurt,” at Vice News Tonight. The series highlights communities impacted by the opioid epidemic, and a 24-minute special report “Committed: Kids & the Mental Health Crisis.” Her photography has been exhibited internationally and recognized by various leaders in photojournalism including Getty Images, Instagram, and the National Press Photographers Association. She holds a masters degree from Columbia Journalism School’s Stabile Center for Investigative Reporting.

people.name: Delphine Halgand-Mishra
people.bio: Delphine Halgand-Mishra is the Executive Director of The Signals Network, a French-American non-profit organization that supports whistleblowers. She served for six years as Reporters Without Borders’ North America Director, advocating for journalists, bloggers, and media rights worldwide. Delphine regularly appears on American and foreign media, and gives lectures and conferences at universities on issues of press freedom violations. Since graduating from Sciences Po Paris with an M.A. in Journalism, Delphine has worked as an economics correspondent for various French media (such as Le Monde, Les Echos, L’Express), focusing mainly on international politics and macroeconomic issues.

people.name: Sally Hayden
people.bio: Sally Hayden is an Irish journalist focused on migration, human rights and humanitarian crises in efforts to exploit corruption by staff within the United Nations Refugee Agency. She has reported across many international outlets including BBC, Al Jazeera, CNN International and the Irish Times. Her latest series, ‘Asylum For Sale’ was funded by Journalists for Transparency, and focused on Kenya and Uganda. She received first prize in the European Migration Media Awards, best ‘foreign coverage’ at the Newsbrands Irish Journalism Awards, and was a finalist for the Amnesty International Gaby Rado Award for Best New Journalist, the Kurt Schork Awards for International Journalism, and other prestigious awards.

people.name: Hannah Hearn
people.bio: Hannah Hearn is the Impact Coordinator for Working Films. She holds a B.A in Film Studies and a Minor in Entrepreneurship from the University of North Carolina Wilmington. Most recently, she was the Managing Director of Visions Film Festival & Conference and the Sound Mixer for the feature-length documentary “Dead in the Water” - a film that exposes the harmful practices of factory farms in eastern NC. In her current role, she is dedicated to coordinating impactful documentary film campaigns both locally and nationally in order to mobilize communities to create a healthy, fair, and equitable world.

people.name: Julia Lowrie Henderson
people.bio: Julia Lowrie Henderson is a graduate of the Salt Institute for Documentary Studies. Her radio work has been featured on Studio 360, Maine Public Broadcasting Network, New Hampshire Public Radio, Public Radio Remix, Sirius XM, ESPN, and more. She is a founding producer of ESPN's 30 for 30 Podcasts, and has produced both of their breakout serialized seasons: Bikram and The Sterling Affairs. Her work for ESPN has been nominated for an IDA Award for Best Audio Documentary. Prior to that, she was an associate producer at WNYC’s Studio 360, where she was awarded a 2016 New York Press Club Award. She holds a BFA in theatre from Boston University. She is a radio producer, documentarian, storyteller, actor, and playwright.

people.name: Angela M. Hill
people.bio: Angela M. Hill is a national investigative producer for the Scripps Washington Bureau and Newsy, where she reports, produces and writes national television, digital and audio stories. Prior to joining Scripps, Angela was a producer with ABC News’ Investigative Unit based in New York. There she reported and produced stories for World News Tonight, Good Morning America, Nightline, 20/20 and ABCNews.com. Angela’s investigative work has led to congressional hearings, changes in laws and institutional reforms. She has won two Emmy Awards, two Peabody Awards, a George Polk Award, an Edward R. Murrow Award and others.

people.name: Harlo Holmes
people.bio: Harlo Holmes is the Director of Newsroom Digital Security at Freedom of the Press Foundation. She strives to help individual journalists in various media organizations become confident and effective in securing their communications within their newsrooms, with their sources, and with the public at large. She is a media scholar, software programmer, and activist.

people.name: Melissa J. Houghton
people.bio: Melissa J. Houghton joined Women in Film & Video (WIFV) as Executive Director in August 2005. Since that time, membership has grown to more than 1,000 media professionals; program provision now averages 70 professional development offerings per year along with the Image Makers program for high school students and the Kids World Film Festival for 5th graders. Houghton has served on the boards of the DC Architectural Foundation, DC Film Alliance, and Wide Angle Youth Media. She is currently a member of the WETA Community Council, the FAVS Advisory Board at George Mason University and the Advisory Board for The Actors’ Center.

people.name: Mary Inman
people.bio: Mary Inman is a partner in Constantine Cannon’s London Office. She specializes in representing whistleblowers from the U.K., Europe and worldwide under the various American whistleblower reward programs, including the federal and various state False Claims Acts and the SEC, CFTC, IRS and DOT whistleblower programs. Inman's successful representation of three whistleblowers exposing fraud in the Medicare Advantage program was featured in a recent New Yorker magazine article. She is a recognized expert and frequent author and speaker on areas related to the application of the American whistleblower laws internationally and the use of whistleblower laws worldwide.

people.name: Jason Fitzroy Jeffers
people.bio: Jason Fitzroy Jeffers is a Barbadian filmmaker and writer whose work has appeared in the Miami Herald and at film festivals such as Sundance and TIFF. Jason is also the co-founder and co-executive director of the Miami-based Caribbean filmmaking and arts collective Third Horizon. Its annual Third Horizon Film Festival celebrates and empowers the new creatives emerging from the region.

people.name: Will Jenkins
people.bio: Will Jenkins has nearly a decade of communications and policy experience at the White House, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and both houses of Congress. He has served as a spokesperson to national and foreign news outlets on a wide range of issues. As a legislative aide in Congress, he guided from introduction to enactment the first legislation to protect American military members from the health effects of toxic burn pits in Iraq and Afghanistan, which has been called “this generation’s Agent Orange.” Over the years, he has worked with dozens of filmmakers to help them understand and engage the policymaking process. He also wrote a guide to politics for filmmakers for Documentary magazine.

people.name: Sylvia Johnson
people.bio: Sylvia Johnson is a filmmaker and impact strategist. She currently splits her time as Creative Director between Free Roaming Studios, a small production company dedicated to visual storytelling to inspire action, and the Santa Fe Dreamers Project, a non-profit immigration legal services organization. Sylvia uses visual storytelling to increase understanding of our shared humanity and connection to the natural world. Her work has screened at film festivals, US Congress, the Department of Interior, and dozens of universities and civic institutions. She is currently a National Geographic Explorer for her upcoming film project, Mermaids Against Plastic.
people.affiliation: Free Roaming Studios / Santa Fe Dreamers Project

people.name: Barbara Kopple
people.bio: Barbara Kopple two-time Academy Award-winning documentarian, is one of the most respected and accomplished filmmakers working today. Barbara’s two Oscars for Harlan County, USA and American Dream make her the only woman filmmaker honored by the Academy with duplicate wins. Her unique ability to capture authentic human moments places her films beyond category, documenting subjects as diverse as Woody Allen on tour with his jazz band in Wild Man Blues, Mike Tyson’s story in Fallen Champ, and the Dixie Chicks in Shut Up and Sing. Barbara’s most recent documentary projects include, Hot Type: 150 Years of the Nation about America’s oldest continuously published weekly magazine, and Miss Sharon Jones!

people.name: Sarah Larson
people.bio: Sarah Larson is a staff writer at The New Yorker. She covers a wide range of cultural subjects, including pop music, television, theatre, and books, and writes Podcast Dept., a weekly column about podcasts, for newyorker.com.

people.name: Luke Lorentzen
people.bio: Luke Lorentzen is a filmmaker and producer whose work explores elements of everyday life questioning and experimenting with the ways in which non-fiction stories are told. His first film, Santa Cruz del Islote (2014) won awards at over ten international film festivals including the San Francisco International, Full Frame Documentary and Chicago International. His undergraduate thesis, New York Cuts (2015), premiered at the International Documentary Festival Amsterdam and Camden International Film Festival. Midnight Family (2019), which tells the story of a family-run ambulance business in Mexico City, won a Special Jury Award for Cinematography at the Sundance Film Festival.

people.name: Wesley Lowery
people.bio: Wesley Lowery is a Pulitzer Prize-winning national correspondent covering law enforcement, race and justice for The Washington Post and an on-air contributor for CNN. He has been the paper’s lead reporter covering police shootings and the Black Lives Matter protest movement. His work has also appeared in the Boston Globe, the Los Angeles Times, the Wall Street Journal and Sports Illustrated. His first book, the New York Times bestseller They Can’t Kill Us All, was awarded the 2017 Christopher Isherwood prize for autobiographical prose by the Los Angeles Times Book Prizes.

people.name: Carrie Lozano
people.bio: Carrie Lozano is director of IDA's Enterprise Documentary Fund, and is a lecturer at UC Berkeley's Graduate School of Journalism Documentary Program. She was previously executive producer for documentaries at Al Jazeera America and senior producer of the network’s investigative series Fault Lines, where her team garnered numerous awards, including an Emmy, a Peabody, and several Headliner Awards. Prior to AJAM, she was director of operations for New Day Films..

people.name: Maren Machles
people.bio: Maren Machles is an investigative journalist whose natural curiosity leads her investigate systemic issues. She has a passion for telling important stories that hold people accountable in a way that makes people think differently. Maren is currently a national investigative associate producer for Newsy and the E.W. Scripps Company, where she creates long-from investigative work with her team members. Prior to her role on the investigative team, she received her Bachelor of Science in journalism at the E.W. Scripps School of Journalism at Ohio University in 2016. During her studies, she had internships with the Scripps Howard Foundation Wire, Narrative.ly and the Long Beach Post.

people.name: Palika Makam
people.bio: Palika Makam has produced video advocacy campaigns and trained activists in using video as a tool for justice all over the world. Additionally, she is the US Senior Program Coordinator at WITNESS and uses her advocacy to lead a project (Eyes on ICE) that supports directly impacted immigrant communities and allies to document abuses by ICE and Border Patrol. Palika is also the cofounder of The Babel Project – a nonprofit that teaches youth activists to use storytelling and documentary film to advocate for their communities and specific policy change.

people.name: Olivia Martin
people.bio: Olivia Martin is a Digital Security Trainer at Freedom of the Press Foundation, where she trains members of the media on digital security awareness. A graduate of NYU's Gallatin School of Individualized Study, her professional work focuses on researching and delivering digital security trainings to journalists, activists, and human rights defenders. She has spent years in newsrooms as a designer and editor with new media and student publications, and uses this experience to aid in assessing the evolving needs of journalists in today's media landscape.

people.name: Eric Matthies
people.bio: Eric Matthies is a cross-platform creative who believes that artistic expression is a vital means of addressing critical issues and that storytelling is a powerful tool for improving the world in which we live. He has worked as a director and producer across a number of genres - from large scale installations to major motion pictures, broadcast specials, web series, multi-platform content packages, site-based VR, world-building R&D, live events and traditional documentaries. Through a combination of rigorous investigative research, Eric’s current focus is on work that contributes to the betterment of our culture, our society, and our planet.

people.name: Debra McClutchy
people.bio: Debra McClutchy is an independent filmmaker based in Brooklyn, NY. she was co-producer of The Booksellers, a documentary about the New York rare book world. She’s also a senior creative producer at Oscilloscope Laboratories, a film distribution company in New York City. Debra joined Oscilloscope in 2009 and produces home video extra features and digital content such as The House that Yauch Built, an online, multimedia experience about the company. Previously, she was a producer for The Criterion Collection, and an associate producer in documentary television in San Francisco, where she won an Emmy Award for A Matter of Seconds, a program about the 1989 earthquake.

people.name: Ivy Meeropol
people.bio: Ivy Meeropol directed and produced the HBO documentary BULLY. COWARD. VICTIM. THE STORY OF ROY COHN, which will premiere at the 2019 New York Film Festival. Also two short films for the Emmy Award-winning documentary series YEARS OF LIVING DANGEROUSLY, and INDIAN POINT. She was the senior story producer for the 2017 CNN Films feature-length documentary THE END: THE FINAL DAYS INSIDE THE OBAMA WHITE HOUSE. Other litany of work include DEATH ROW STORIES, THE HILL, and HEIR TO AN EXECUTION, which explored the legacy of her grandparents, Ethel and Julius Rosenberg.

people.name: Dana Merwin
people.bio: Dana Merwin is the Program Officer at the International Documentary Association. Prior to joining IDA, Dana was the production manager for Al Jazeera America's documentary unit and the Peabody Award winning series Fault Lines. She was the Director of Operations for Jupiter Entertainment in Los Angeles, where she oversaw delivery of docu-reality series to various cable channels. She has served as a production manager on numerous film and television productions.

people.name: Emily Michot
people.bio: Emily Michot has been a staff photographer and videographer at the Miami Herald. Michot has worked as the visual journalist with the Miami Herald’s I-Team on some of their most acclaimed projects, including License to Launder and Fight Club, that won Pulitzer-prize. This past year, Michot spent a year working on interviewing young women who were sexually abused by multimillionaire Jeffrey Epstein. The series, Perversion of Justice, examined how Alexander Acosta, a future Trump Cabinet member, gave Epstein a secret plea deal that allowed him to escape a life sentence in federal prison. Epstein was arrested eight months after the series ran, and was later found dead in his jail cell from what has been ruled a suicide.

people.name: Alexander A. Mora
people.bio: Alexander A. Mora is a first-time filmmaker with a background in architecture, policy and the law. Keenly interested in international rights-based advocacy, he was an active member on the board of Yale Law School’s Human Rights and Development Journal before directing “The Nightcrawlers.” His persistent desire to find greater synergy between his passion for creative storytelling and his dedication to rights-based advocacy led to his first foray into narrative documentary filmmaking.

people.name: Tom Mueller
people.bio: Tom Mueller is a New York Times-bestselling author and reporter. He has reported from 22 countries on a wide range of topics, with recent emphasis on fraud and institutional corruption. His latest book is Crisis of Conscience: Whistleblowing in an Age of Fraud, traces the rise of whistleblowing as a legal and social phenomenon. It also explores the societal, economic and psychological drivers of whistleblowing, which include institutional corruption, revolving door and other extreme conflict of interest situations, the cult of secrecy and the psychoactive nature of money.

people.name: Molly Murphy
people.bio: Molly Murphy co-directs Working Films, a nonprofit organization that uses documentary film to advance social justice and environmental protection. In her eighteen year tenure, she has planned and directed national media engagement campaigns, facilitated partnerships and coordinated coalitions centered on the use of documentaries to enhance communication. Molly has designed and led dozens of trainings for filmmakers, grassroots organizations, and NGOs focused on using film and online media to effect change. She leads the Docs In Action initiative for Working Films, which provides finishing funds to short films and campaign strategy development at no cost to underrepresented documentary makers.

people.name: Jacqueline Olive
people.bio: Jacqueline Olive is an independent filmmaker and immersive media producer with more than a decade of experience in journalism and film. Her debut feature documentary, Always in Season, premiered at the 2019 Sundance Film Festival and was awarded the Special Jury Prize for Moral Urgency. Jackie also co-directed and co-produced the award-winning thesis film, Black to Our Roots, which broadcast on PBS WORLD in 2009. Prior to that, Jackie is producing an accompanying VR project that uses 360° video and computer-generated imagery (CGI) animation offering users strategies for moving confidently through the racialized public spaces that black women navigate daily.

people.name: Lauren Pabst
people.bio: Lauren Pabst is a Senior Program Officer in the Journalism and Media program at the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation. In this role, she is involved in organizations’ funding of professional nonprofit reporting, nonfiction multimedia storytelling and participatory civic media. Previously she worked with the Rada Film Group, Black Public Media, and Public Policy Productions.
people.affiliation: John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation

people.name: Janice Page
people.bio: Janice Page is the Arts Editor at The Washington Post. She was previously Deputy Managing Editor for Arts and Newsroom Innovation at The Boston Globe, where she led efforts to expand the reach of The Globe’s journalism through book, film and television deals, podcasts and live events. Janice has had a long, distinguished career in features editing. She was a reporter and arts and entertainment editor at the Los Angeles Times and the executive producer of the Boston site of MSN/Sidewalk.com. She got her start in features at the Providence Journal-Bulletin.

people.name: Andrea Passafiume
people.bio: Andrea Passafiume is the Program Manager for Docs In Progress, where she is responsible for managing the organization's educational and professional development programs for adults and youth. Concurrently, she is Assistant Programmer of documentaries for the Tribeca Film Festival. She has served on the Screening Committees for DOC NYC and Camden International Film Festival as well as numerous film juries and panels. Passafiume is also a regular contributing writer for Turner Classic Movies and FilmStruck, and co-wrote the tribute book for the AFI Life Achievement Award presented to Steve Martin in 2015.

people.name: Amanda Pike
people.bio: Amanda Pike leads the TV and documentary department at The Center for Investigative Reporting, developing and overseeing CIR's documentary films and series as well as TV news reports and animated shorts. Under her leadership, The Center for Investigative Reporting garnered its first Academy Award nomination, a duPont and four national Emmys, among other accolades. She was the executive producer of the inaugural year of the Glassbreaker Films initiative, supporting women in documentary filmmaking and investigative journalism. Previously, she spent the last 15 years reporting and producing documentaries for PBS, CBS, ABC, National Geographic, and The Learning Channel, among others.

people.name: Courtney C. Radsch
people.bio: Courtney C. Radsch, Ph.D, is advocacy director at the Committee to Protect Journalists. She serves as chief spokesperson on global press freedom issues for the organization and oversees CPJ's engagement on other multilateral institutions as well as CPJ's campaigns on behalf of journalists killed and imprisoned for their work. As a veteran journalist, researcher, and free expression advocate, she frequently writes and speaks about the intersection of media, technology, and human rights. Radsch worked for UNESCO, edited the flagship publication "World Trends in Freedom of Expression and Media Development," and managed the Global Freedom of Expression Campaign at Freedom House.

people.name: Sara Rafsky
people.bio: Sara Rafsky is the Safe+Secure Executive-at-large at Doc Society and a Senior Research Fellow at the Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia at University. She was previously a researcher at the Open Documentary Lab at MIT, where she received her MS in Comparative Media Studies, and a Google News Lab Fellow at Witness. Prior to that she was the Researcher on Central America at Amnesty International in Mexico City and the Americas Research Associate for the Committee to Protect Journalists in New York, where she reported on press freedom and human rights issues in the United States and Latin America.

people.name: Susanne Reber
people.bio: Susanne Reber is an award-winning investigative editor, executive producer and author. She is currently leading the podcast team at the E. W. Scripps Washington Bureau. Her work has garnered her three Peabody Awards, an Emmy award, and a DuPont award, among many others, and has been showcased in national and international film festivals. She is the co-founder of Reveal and the former executive editor of the Peabody Award-winning investigative radio program and podcast. Prior to joining Scripps she held leadership roles at The Center for Investigative Reporting.

people.name: Heidi Reinberg
people.bio: Heidi Reinberg is currently producing the UNTITLED CRIMINAL JUSTICE / HS PROJECT alongside that film’s director, Emmy winner Maisie Crow. Additionally, she served as Consulting Producer on director Tania Cypriano’s Born to Be, which will premiere at this fall’s New York Film Festival. Reinberg produced the ITVS co-production 93Queen, which won the inaugural Hot Docs Forum first look Pitch Prize before premiering at the Hot Docs Documentary Festival. Most recently, Reinberg worked with Oscar winners Ross Kauffman and Cynthia Wade, and award-winning directors Mai Iskander and Jeremiah Zagar.

people.name: Jay Rosen
people.bio: Jay Rosen has been teaching journalism at New York University since 1986. He is the author of PressThink, a blog about journalism and its ordeals. In 1999, Yale University Press published his book, What Are Journalists For?, which is about the rise of the civic journalism movement during the pre-internet era. In 2017 he became director of the Membership Puzzle Project, funded by the Knight Foundation, Democracy Fund, and Luminate. It studies membership models for sustainability in the news. Rosen is also an active press critic with a focus on problems in the coverage of politics.

people.name: Kenneth Rosenberg
people.bio: Dr. Kenneth Rosenberg has been making award-winning documentaries for over thirty years. Aired on PBS, he co-produced and co-directed (with Ruth Neuwald Falcon) An Alzheimer’s Story and directed and produced Through Madness. For HBO, he produced and directed Coming Out In America (Oscar short list), Back from Madness, Drinking Apart, and Executive-Produced the Peabody Award-winning Cancer: Evolution To Revolution. A practicing psychiatrist and author of medical textbooks, his films have been recognized by the American Medical Association, the American Psychiatric Association, the National Institute on Drug Abuse, the New England Journal of Medicine, the National Alliance for the Mentally Ill, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.

people.name: Tina Rosenberg
people.bio: Tina Rosenberg is co-writer of the New York Times Fixes column and co-founder of the Solutions Journalism Network. She is a longtime New York Times writer, for the editorial page and Sunday magazine as well as Fixes. She has written hundreds of magazine articles for publications such as The New Yorker, The Atlantic and Rolling Stone as well as the Times Sunday magazine. She has also written three books: Children of Cain: Violence and the Violent in Latin America; The Haunted Land: Facing Europe's Ghosts After Communism; and Join the Club: How Peer Pressure Can Transform the World. She won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award for Haunted Land.

people.name: Felix Salmon
people.bio: Felix Salmon, the chief financial correspondent at Axios, is an award-winning writer, editor, and podcaster. The host of the weekly Slate Money podcast, he was previously the finance blogger at Roubini Global Economics, Condé Nast Portfolio, and Reuters.

people.name: Juliana Schatz
people.bio: Juliana Schatz is a documentary film producer and director. In 2018 she was nominated for a Livingston Award for Young Journalists. Juliana started her career at the award-winning investigative series Frontline, where she contributed to 11 public affairs documentaries -- including two Emmy Award winners and one Peabody Award winner. Her work with PBS FRONTLINE, The GroundTruth Project, Al Jazeera and Sender Films has taken her from the peaks of Giza to the sky-high Rocky Mountains.

people.name: Hilke Schellmann
people.bio: Hilke Schellmann is an assistant professor of journalism at New York University and an Emmy-award winning investigative reporter. She is currently a showrunner and reporter for The Wall Street Journal's high-profile video series Moving Upstream. As an independent filmmaker, Schellmann shot, produced and directed the investigative documentary Outlawed in Pakistan, which aired on FRONTLINE. The documentary was recognized with an Emmy, an Overseas Press Club and a Cinema for Peace Award.

people.name: Gunita Singh
people.bio: Gunita Singh is the Jack Nelson/Dow Jones Foundation Legal Fellow at the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, where she assists with litigation and amicus work with a focus on FOIA and public records. Prior to joining the Reporters Committee, she was a staff attorney at Property of the People, a DC-based nonprofit that uses FOIA to foster transparency and accountability. She graduated from Georgetown University Law Center in 2017.
people.affiliation: Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press

people.name: Andalusia Knoll Soloff
people.bio: Andalusia Knoll Soloff is an award-winning multimedia journalist based in Mexico City, and a freelance video producer for Al Jazeera, Democracy Now!, VICE News, BBC, ZDF, TeleSUR, and NBC Latino. Her reporting focuses on human resilience and dignity in the face of disappearances, state violence, land struggles and gender-based murders in Latin America. She is the founder and coordinator of the new journalist organization, Frontline Freelance México, collaborates with the Mexican Periodistas de a Pie network and has been active in the press freedom movement in Mexico. She is the author of the graphic novel Alive You Took Them, about the 43 disappeared Ayotzinapa students.

people.name: Courtney Symone Staton
people.bio: Courtney Symone Staton, lead producer of “Silence Sam” from Greenville NC, is an activist who uses poetry, film and photography to celebrate the everyday heroism in protest and black identity. She serves as a lead producer and impact producer of “Silence Sam,” a participatory documentary about the student-led movement to remove Confederate monument “Silent Sam” from the campus of the University of North Carolina - Chapel Hill and the resulting silencing of student activism. A 2018 Next Doc Fellow, she uses her art to drive viewers past the point of empathy to the point of healing and action.

people.name: Michèle Stephenson
people.bio: Michèle Stephenson, co-founding member of the Rada Film Group, filmmaker, artist and author, pulls from her Panamanian and Haitian roots and international experience as a human rights attorney to tell provocative stories in a variety of media that speak to personal and systemic liberation. Her work has appeared on a variety of broadcast and web platforms, including PBS, Showtime and MTV. Her documentary,”American Promise,”was nominated for three Emmys including Best Documentary and Best News Coverage of a Contemporary Issue. The film also won the Jury Prize at Sundance, and was selected for the New York Film Festivals’ Main Slate Program.

people.name: Jeffrey Sterling
people.bio: Jeffrey Sterling is former CIA case officer who was wrongfully convicted of violating the Espionage Act. Working for nearly a decade, Jeffrey sued the agency for racial discrimination, and also went through proper channels to tell both Congressional intelligence committees about the discrimination he faced at the CIA and about a botched and dangerous covert operation. His discrimination suit was not allowed to go forward as the government successfully argued it posed a threat to national security.After released from prison in 2018, he advocates in his book, Unwanted Spy - The Persecution of an American Whistleblower, expected on October 15, 2019.

people.name: Ricki Stern
people.bio: Directors and writers Ricki Stern and Annie Sundberg are the leading creative forces behind Break Thru Films and are known for crafting deft and cinematic journeys through unexpected territory. Break Thru Films recently completed a 5-part documentary series for AMC that explores the 1986 murder of Jennifer Levin in New York City and the trial that ensued for Robert Chambers in “Preppy Murder: Death in Central Park.” Other films include: Joan Rivers – A Piece of Work (2010), The Devil Came On Horseback (2008) and The Trials of Darryl Hunt (2007).

people.name: Annie Sundberg
people.bio: Directors and writers Ricki Stern and Annie Sundberg are the leading creative forces behind Break Thru Films and are known for crafting deft and cinematic journeys through unexpected territory. Break Thru Films recently completed a 5-part documentary series for AMC that explores the 1986 murder of Jennifer Levin in New York City and the trial that ensued for Robert Chambers in “Preppy Murder: Death in Central Park.” Other films include: Joan Rivers – A Piece of Work (2010), The Devil Came On Horseback (2008) and The Trials of Darryl Hunt (2007).

people.name: Joel Stonington
people.bio: Joel Stonington has worked in journalism for more than a decade, writing about energy, crime, politics and other topics. He has previously reported for The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, Los Angeles Times, The Guardian, New York Magazine, Bloomberg Businessweek, Der Spiegel, MSNBC and ABC News. Stonington has received fellowships and funding to support reporting from the Kiplinger Program in Public Affairs Journalism, Humboldt Foundation and Carnegie Corporation.

people.name: Jess Swanson
people.bio: Jess Swanson is the senior editor of American Airlines' American Way and Celebrated Living magazines, and a part-time lecturer at the University of Miami. A graduate of Columbia University School of Journalism, she has written for Fort Lauderdale Magazine, Venice, Miami New Times and the Village Voice.
people.affiliation: American Way and Celebrated Living magazines

people.name: Emily Taguchi
people.bio: Emily Taguchi is a producer for Nightline, and a filmmaker whose work has been recognized with multiple Emmy nominations and a duPont-Columbia Award. Her most recent film, "After Parkland," premiered at the Tribeca Film Festival this year and continues screening at festivals around the country. She produced films Taller Than The Trees (AFI, Tribeca) and Growing Up Trans. Her next project with co-director Jake Lefferman, follows the journeys of asylum seekers from Central America.Born in Tokyo, Japan, Emily graduated from Tufts University and the Graduate School of Journalism at the University of California at Berkeley.

people.name: Zach Toombs
people.bio: Zach Toombs is a reporter and documentary producer. He heads up the Newsy Documentaries unit, with projects on Prime Video and Hulu. His work has been recognized with an Emmy nomination and 2 National Murrow Awards.

people.name: Jenn Topper
people.bio: Jenn Topper, the communications director for Reporters Committee, oversees the development of communications and messaging strategies to advance the RCFP mission and leads efforts to engage more people with the organization’s work. Prior to joining the Reporters Committee, Jenn was the communications director at the Sunlight Foundation, an organization that worked to make government more transparent and accountable. In addition to leading Sunlight’s communications team, Jenn oversaw the organization’s strategy around the 2016 election and managed key projects on anti-corruption efforts and criminal justice reform.
people.affiliation: Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press

people.name: Yatziri Tovar
people.bio: Yatziri Tovar was born in Mexico and migrated to the Bronx in New York City with her family when she was a toddler. Yatziri became a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient in 2013. She has previously worked as a college counselor helping immigrant youth navigate the college application process, interned at the office of a private immigration attorney and worked at the Consulate General of Mexico in New York. At the same time, she continued her advocacy work as a member of Make the Road New York (MRNY), where she has spoke at various press conferences and rallies. Since then she has appeared in both local and national news outlets to share her experiences as an immigrant, student, and activist.

people.name: Katie Townsend
people.bio: Katie Townsend is the Litigation Director at the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press an unincorporated nonprofit association of reporters and editors based in Washington, D.C. Townsend oversees the direct litigation work of RCFP attorneys, and represents RCFP, news organizations, and individual journalists. Before, Townsend was an associate in the Los Angeles office of Gibson Dunn & Crutcher LLP, where she specialized in media and entertainment litigation. She was named part of the "Next Gen - Hollywood's Up-and-Coming Execs 35 and Under" by the Hollywood Reporter.
people.affiliation: Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press

people.name: Christiaan Triebert
people.bio: Christiaan Triebert is an award-winning investigative journalist on the Visual Investigations team at The New York Times. Triebert worked as a senior investigator and lead trainer at the investigative group Bellingcat, which ranged from a variety of countries including Asia, the Middle East, Europe and Latin America. In 2017, he won a European Press Prize Innovation Award for his reconstruction of the attempted military coup in Turkey using leaked WhatsApp messages and social media content. In 2018, Triebert worked with the World Press Photo Foundation to fact-check and verify each and every winning image and its captions of for the world’s leading photojournalism contest.

people.name: Lea Trusty
people.bio: Lea Trusty is a program assistant at the Democracy Fund, a bipartisan foundation working to ensure that our political system is able to withstand new challenges and deliver on its promise to the American people. Trusty supports the Public Square Program in its mission to invest in innovations and institutions that focus on creating audience-centered, trusted, resilient newsrooms that reflect the diversity of their communities. She co-leads Democracy Fund’s Engaged Journalism strategy with Paul Waters.

people.name: Nicole Tsien
people.bio: Nicole Tsien is the Co-Producer at POV. As a member of the programming and production team, she manages film submissions, oversees pre-screeners, and contributes to the curation and production of the series

people.name: Michelle Vaughan
people.bio: Michelle Vaughan grew up surrounded by art. She spent 3 years in a traditional program until moving to a conceptual one at UCLA. That education shaped her approach to art and she got to study under many accomplished artists. After graduating, Michelle took more technical art classes and continues to learn new skills when necessary. She is a project-based artist primarily making drawings and prints but will expand into various mediums and sometimes collaborate with other artists. Topics include politics, history and art history, sociology, science and occasionally food. Michelle lives with her husband, Felix Salmon, in a Brutalist tower in Chinatown, NYC.

people.name: Orlando von Einsiedel
people.bio: Orlando von Einsiedel is the multi-award-winning director of the Oscar-nominated Netflix short documentary, “The White Helmets.” His first feature, the BAFTA- and Academy Award- nominated documentary “Virunga,” won more than 50 international honors, including an Emmy, a Peabody, a Grierson and a DuPont-Columbia Award for outstanding journalism. Einsiedel is drawn to telling inspiring human narratives from around the world, frequently combining intimate personal stories with powerful visual aesthetics and in-depth investigations. He has worked in every continent, often in impenetrable and difficult environments, from pirate boats to war zones.

people.name: Chloe Walters Wallace
people.bio: Chloe Walters Wallace is the manager of the Firelight Media Documentary Lab, a fellowship that provides mentorship, funding, and access to first- and second-time filmmakers from racially and ethnically underrepresented communities, as well as “Groundwork,” a new Firelight initiative, which aims to expand the pipeline of emerging independent filmmakers from the South and the Midwest by providing an introduction to the opportunities across the documentary landscape.

people.name: Nanfu Wang
people.bio: Nanfu Wang is a Chinese filmmaker based in New York City. She directed and produced feature documentaries Hooligan Sparrow, I Am Another You and One Child Nation. Wang is the recipient of two Emmy nominations, an Independent Spirit Award, a Peabody Award, Cinema Eye Honor, George Polk Award, IDA award, and 20 other honors. Originally from a remote village in China, Wang overcame poverty and a lack of access to formal education en route to earning her master’s, in which she teaches cinematography and editing at one of the three universities she studied at, New York University.

people.name: Claire Wardle
people.bio: Claire Wardle currently leads the strategic direction and research for First Draft. In 2017 she co-authored the seminal report, Information Disorder: An interdisciplinary Framework for Research and Policy for the Council of Europe. Previous to that she was a Fellow at the Shorenstein Center for Media, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard’s Kennedy School, the Research Director at the Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism and head of social media for the United Nations Refugee Agency.

people.name: Aisha White
people.bio: Aisha White is the Program Manager for Halcyon Arts Lab where she works to build bridges for artist looking to make an impact within their communities. Her background in community engagement and sustainable development has informed her passion for socially engaged art. As Program Manager she works with socially and civically engaged artist to help grow their practices and impact. She has 6 years of experience in cultural policy, international development, arts administration and social enterprise. She holds a B.A. in Business Administration from the Universities of Pittsburgh and an interdisciplinary degree in Arts, Enterprise and Development from the Center for Cultural and Media Policy Studies at the University of Warwick.

people.name: Marco Williams
people.bio: Marco Williams is an award-winning documentary filmmaker and professor of film production at New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts. He has been nominated three times for the Sundance Film Festival grand jury prize. Williams’ most recent completed film is “The Undocumented,” a PBS broadcast/Independent Lens feature-length cinema verite documentary addressing the deaths of illegal border crossers in Arizona’s border region.
people.affiliation: New York University Tisch School of the Arts

people.name: Shayna Wilson
people.bio: Shayna Wilson currently serves in a dual role as an Independent Living Advocate for the deaf & hard of hearing at The Independence Unlimited Center, and as a Vocational Advocate for the deaf and hard of hearing for the Disabilities Network of Eastern Connecticut. Shayna began learning American sign language while taking parent sign language classes at the school for the deaf when her daughter was just 3 years old in 2004. Shayna is the founder of a community-based organization called NexIzNow, an organization that promotes advocacy through a holistic perspective in the greater Hartford area and abroad. Shayna remains passionate about advocacy for all families with children with disabilities.

people.name: Lisa Zycherman
people.bio: Lisa Zycherman represents and counsels clients on a wide range of issues in First Amendment, media and intellectual property law, including libel, copyright, trademark, right of publicity, privacy and newsgathering matters. Zycherman also advises newspaper, magazine, website, television, film and book-publishing clients on pre-publication and pre-broadcast legal issues.
